newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn urged not to force Bosnian refugees home.
newsitem.headline: Bonn urged not to force Bosnian refugees home.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency appealed on Monday to Germany's regional states not to start forcing some 320,000 Bosnian refugees to return to their war-devastated country on Tuesday.

Judith Kumin, the U.N. High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) representative in Bonn, said Germany had wrongly interpreted a U.N. report on Bosnia and insisted that no areas were entirely safe for refugees' return regardless of their ethnic origin.
She urged Germany to provide more financial aid for post-war reconstruction and said this was the best way of persuading them to return of their own accord.

But Bonn hardened its resolve to speed the return of refugees to their homeland when the development ministry announced it would open an employment agency on Tuesday to help refugees find work before they go home.
"The work of refugees living in Germany is vitally needed for reconstruction," Development Minister Carl-Dieter Spranger said in a statement.

"Who apart from the Bosnians themselves should reconstruct their country? Neither Germany nor the international community can provide the Bosnians with a country that is ready for immediate occupation."
The federal government in Bonn and the country's 16 regional states agreed earlier this year that some refugees could be forced to go home from Tuesday October 1 if they refused to go voluntarily.

Some German regions, including Bavaria and city-state Berlin, have said they will start sending refugees home from Tuesday but others have heeded the advice of refugee agencies, who say they should wait until next spring at the earliest.
German leaders have defended their policy, citing the U.N. report that designated 22 areas in Bosnia as safe. But Kumin said they were mistaken.
"These 22 areas are places that were relatively badly affected by the war, but where a certain number of former inhabitants could return," she told ZDF television.
"Of course it depends on the area, but this list is not a list of safe areas nor a list of places where refugees can return or be forced to return without any problems," she said.
"It is essential to know which ethnic group the refugees belong to decide who can go where. Only then can you draw up plans for their return," she said.

Kumin said it was too early for compulsory repatriation because it was only safe enough for refugees to return to areas dominated by their own ethnic group. Mixed marriage couples still did not know where to go, she said.

She also warned that the threat of possible forced repatriation could lead to thousands of Bosnian refugees migrating across Germany to other regional states which have said they will not start forcing refugees home yet.
Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel gave assurances earlier this month that there would be no heartless repatriations.
